description: We are a group of data analytics students, we are really interested in astrophysics and like to eat donuts. We have skills in many programming languages additionally we are good with numbers and design.
summary:
Sakipa Satellite is a strategy card game for 1–4 players, playable in the browser. Each player runs a small space agency: take a science mission, pick an orbit, build a CubeSat from real parts (frames, solar panels, cameras, antennas, thrusters), launch it, and score Science Points from the data it sends home.

It answers the Space Mission Design challenge by turning the real design loop into play. Every choice trades cost, science and risk, shown live on a Trade Space meter. A design review checks size, power, instruments and comms before launch. Orbits change launch cost, sunlight, risk and signal speed, and the orbit map shows their real distances. After each mission, a debrief compares your design with cheaper and safer alternatives. In co-op mode, the group builds one flagship observatory together, each agency owning a subsystem.

It matters because spacecraft engineering feels out of reach for most people. Here, players learn by doing why you can't max out everything at once, and every mission, orbit and part card links to the published science behind it.
details:
Sakipa Satellite is a strategy card game about designing space missions, for 1 to 4 players. It works as a printed deck and as a browser game. Each player runs a small space agency. On a turn you take a science mission (tracking wildfires, mapping the Moon's magnetism, watching distant nebulae), choose an orbit, and build a CubeSat from real types of parts: frames, solar cells and panels, batteries, cameras, radios, thrusters, reaction wheels and radiation shielding. Before launch, a design review checks that everything fits the frame, that the satellite makes more power than it uses, and that it has the right instrument, antenna and propulsion for its orbit. Then you launch, roll against the satellite's risk, collect data each round, send it home through your antenna, and earn Science Points. The first agency to 10 points wins, or the leader after six rounds.

Every decision is a trade-off between cost, science return and risk, shown live on each player's Trade Space meter. Orbits change the launch price, how much sunlight reaches your panels, how risky the launch is, and how often you can send data home. An orbit map shows their real distances and signal delays. Random events (solar flares, budget cuts, launch delays, ground station passes) shake up every round. Players can insure launches, trade parts and money, and share rockets. In co-op mode the whole group builds one flagship observatory together: each agency owns a subsystem, shares one budget, and must meet the highest reliability standard. After each mission, a debrief puts your design on a cost-against-risk chart next to a cheaper and a safer alternative, and explains what real engineers would weigh up.

The benefit is that players learn engineering judgment by doing it rather than reading about it. They discover for themselves why a cheap satellite fails more often, why distant orbits need bigger antennas and better propulsion, and why you can never max out cost, science and risk at once. Every mission, orbit and part card carries a "Real Science" line linking to a published source, so the science is part of play rather than a separate lesson. Our intended impact is to make spacecraft engineering feel reachable for students and the public. The game is meant for classrooms, science clubs and families, playable on one shared device or around a table.

We built the digital version with HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks. It runs in any modern browser with no install or account. The game rules live in a separate JavaScript engine with no screen code, which also runs in Node.js. We used that to build a balance simulator in which computer players play thousands of games. That let us measure and tune the win rate, how fast each orbit pays back, and co-op difficulty with data instead of guesswork. Python and the Pillow imaging library let us update text on the 106 card images, and macOS's built-in text recognition helped us check the card art. We used Git and GitHub for version control and Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.

The creative choice was to turn the real mission design loop into the game's core mechanic. Missions, orbits, design reviews, trade studies, launch risk, downlink limits, launch insurance and post-mission debriefs are how real missions work, not decoration. The visual style borrows from 1970s mission control and vintage space illustration, and the animations (card shuffles, launches, dice rolls, satellites circling the orbit map) make the system easy to read at a glance.

Our team considered several factors throughout:

  • Scientific accuracy: we checked and corrected the science lines.
  • Balance: we tuned every major number with the simulator.
  • Learnability: a guided first satellite shows each new player the next step.
  • Accessibility: everything works with the keyboard, players are marked by shape as well as colour, and motion switches off when reduced motion is turned on.
  • Group play: hot-seat mode works on one shared screen, and a co-op mode suits classrooms.
